full_judgment: 10. Be that as it may, though certain facts and circumstances are to be taken into consideration for determining the actual true nature of a particular receipt, the burden is always on the department to prove that a particular receipt does not fall under the criteria of capital receipts (See Saroj vs CIT 37 ITR-242, 248 (SC)]. It has been held by the Supreme Court of India in one of the latest decisions, namely in CIT vs Karnataka Power, 247 ITR-268 (SC), that if a deposit of money is directly linked with the purchase of plant and machinery or incidental  to the setting up of a plant, the interest thereon received by the assessee is a capital receipt. Again, it was held in CIT vs Karnataka Urban Infrastructure Development & Finance Corporation, 284 ITR-582 that, in computing the total income of the assessee, the interest accrued on bank deposits that were made pending implementation of the schemes could not be treated as income. Therefore, considering the aforesaid decisions of the higher Courts as well as the commentaries of the learned authors in Kanga and Palkhivala's, "The Law and Practice of Income Tax" (10th Edition), Lexis Nexis, under the Chapter- "Tests to-Distinguish Between Capital and Income Receipts", it appears generally that, when a particular fund is kept in the bank account of the assessee, under whatever headings, for the implementation of any project or schemes and any delay takes place in such implantation of the said projects and schemes and, in the meantime, the interest accrues on the said deposit shall be treated to be receipts of capital nature not exigible to tax. Therefore, the intention of the assessee has also to be examined for determination of the nature of deposits as well as the interests accrued thereon, though, generally, the interests accrued on deposits or any amount under a contract, award, decree or other orders are taxable.
